Learning Objectives
Review the clinical presentation of femoral head fractures and the Pipkin classification.
Discuss indications for the surgical management of femoral head fractures and associated
injuries.
Appreciate surgical approaches for the surgical management of femoral head fracture and the
relative advantages and disadvantages of each approach.
Explain fixation strategies for femoral head fractures.
Recognize clinical and radiographic features of irreducible hip dislocations.
Explain characteristic complications that arise after the management of femoral head
fractures.


Introduction
Femoral head fractures are relatively rare injuries that may represent a major
reconstruction challenge. They most frequently result from high-energy trauma in young
patients; however, they also can result from trauma in geriatric patients. Femoral head
fracture is present in as many as 16% of patients with a traumatic posterior hip
dislocation.1-4 Although early clinical series reported relatively poor outcomes,5,6
contemporary approaches focused on anatomic reduction and stable fixation have
reported high union rates for most femoral head fracture subtypes.7
Classification
The Pipkin classification is used to describe subtypes of femoral head fractures and concomitant
injuries6 (Figure 1).
Pipkin type I fractures are infrafoveal.
Pipkin type II fractures are suprafoveal; therefore, the fracture line exits into the primary
weight-bearing surface areas of the femoral head.
Pipkin type III fractures include any femoral head fracture and a concomitant femoral neck
fracture. Beyond representing a surgical challenge in managing two distinct fracture patterns,
type III fractures also portend a poor outcome.7
Pipkin type IV fractures are femoral head fractures with acetabular fractures, typically a
posterior wall fracture. The differences between a type II and a type IV fracture may be subtle
because femoral head fractures are almost always the result of a posteriorly directed
dislocation and, therefore, by definition, a posterior structural injury to the capsulolabral
tissue will be present with potential small posterior wall avulsions, and no clarification in the
Pipkin classification system is available with regard to the minimum size of the posterior wall
fragments to classify it a type IV fracture.

Figure 1 Illustrations show the Pipkin classification.A, Type I, infrafoveal femoral head fracture. B,
Type II, suprafoveal head fracture. C, Type III, any femoral head fracture with an ipsilateral
femoral neck fracture. D, Type IV, any femoral head fracture with an associated posterior wall
fracture. (Courtesy of L. Henry Goodnough, MD, Seattle, WA. Illustration by Sean Daley.)
Indications for Surgical Management

Indications for Surgical Management
Indications for surgical management stem from the goal of restoring a stable and
congruent hip joint. Surgical management is indicated for fractures associated with hip
instability to re-establish physiologic stability. Fragment location and size are important
factors. Surgical fixation is indicated for Pipkin type II fractures, which extend into and
disrupt the primary weight-bearing surface areas of the femoral head, to restore
articular congruity and consequent stability. Pipkin type I fractures, which are infrafoveal,
may be managed nonsurgically, especially if congruency of the hip joint is not
compromised. This is related to the morphology of the acetabulum and relative coverage
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Femoral Head Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004094
3/19

of the femoral head. A stress examination under anesthesia can be performed, similar to
an evaluation for stability in patients with an isolated posterior wall fracture.
Pipkin type III fractures are managed surgically; however, acute arthroplasty may be
indicated, given the poor prognosis.
In type IV fractures, the goals of surgical management are restoration of stability and
articular congruity of the hip and removal of any fragments blocking concentric
reduction of the hip. Independent evaluation of the femoral head and posterior wall
fractures is warranted. Typically (although not always), the femoral head fracture is the
more substantial injury and is addressed primarily. After fixation of the femoral head,
the posterior wall can be fixed routinely or assessed via dynamic fluoroscopy to
determine its role in hip stability.
Surgical Approaches
The two primary surgical approaches can be used.
Anterior: Hueter/Smith-Petersen
Posterior: Kocher-Langenbeck or Gibson with surgical hip dislocation
Anterior Approach
Via a Hueter or Smith-Petersen interval, facilitates direct access to head fragments and
accurate screw trajectories (Videos 1, 2, 3, and 4)
Affords easy access to fracture fragments and placement of fixation and involves a low risk of
disrupting the femoral head blood supply
Anteroinferior fragments often are generated by posterior shear forces of the femoral head
against the posterior acetabulum. Therefore, an anterior exposure affords direct access to
characteristic fracture fragments and a biomechanically sound, anterior-to-posterior screw
trajectory.8

Figure 2 Illustrations of a hip show the anterior approach for the management of femoral neck
fractures. A, Skin incision for the Hueter approach, which is the distal aspect of the Smith-
Petersen approach. B, Superficial dissection, including incision of the tensor fascia. C, Indirect
head of rectus tenotomy. D, Anterior dislocation of the femoral neck for reduction and fixation.
(Courtesy of L. Henry Goodnough, MD, Seattle, WA. Illustration by Sean Daley.)

Anterior Approach
With the patient in the supine position, a skin incision is made 2 cm distal and lateral to
the anterior superior iliac spine and carried distally 10 to 12 cm, in line with the lateral
border of the patella. The tensor fascia is incised, and the interval between the tensor
and the rectus femoris is bluntly developed from within the sheath. The floor of the
sheath is incised, and the ascending branches of the lateral femoral circumflex vessels
are identified and ligated. Lateral retraction of the tensor fascia and medial retraction of
the rectus facilitate access to the anterior hip capsule overlying the femoral neck for an
arthrotomy. Sharp elevation of the iliocapsularis affords full exposure to the anterior
capsule. Release of the reflected (indirect) head of the rectus can provide additional
exposure of the capsule.
Capsulotomy of the anterior hip capsule is then performed. An oblique T-shaped
capsulotomy is created, with the cranial limb parallel to but not violating the acetabular
labrum, and with the caudal limb parallel to the neck. For additional exposure, a
secondary limb along the intertrochanteric line to the lesser trochanter can be added
(Figure 3). The authors of this lesson typically dislocate the femoral head anteriorly to
provide the most direct access for reduction and fixation; however, it is possible to
provide fixation with the head remaining within the acetabulum. If the head is difficult to
dislocate, tenotomy of the direct head of the rectus can be performed, which easily
facilitates dislocation. In addition, cranial release of the superior capsule off the ilium
and complete release of the capsule medially to the lesser trochanter (pubofemoral
ligament) increases the ability to mobilize the femur and dislocate the head.
The Hueter approach also can be extended proximally into the Smith-Petersen
interval.10 Limitations of the anterior approach include inability to access posterior wall

fragments and posterior labrum tears. In addition, a theoretic concern exists that an
anterior approach may disrupt the only remaining blood supply to the femoral head if a
posterior fracture-dislocation were to avulse the dominant posterior-based perfusion;5
however, the literature contains no reports of markedly higher rates of subsequent
osteonecrosis.8,11 In Pipkin type IV fracture-dislocations, the femoral head fracture can
be addressed with the patient in the supine position via an anterior approach, after
which the stability of the hip can be assessed via a dynamic stress examination under
anesthesia. If deemed unstable, reduction and fixation of the wall can subsequently be
performed via a separate posteriorly based approach ( Figure 4).
Figure 3 Illustrations of a hip show the modified Smith-Petersen approach. A, The
superficial plane of the approach. The rec¬tus femoris muscle lies in the interval
between the sartorius muscle, which is innervated by the femoral nerve, and the tensor
fasciae latae muscle, which is innervated by the superior gluteal nerve. B, The surgeon
must avoid injuring the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, which pierces the fascia in the
line between these muscles. C, The rectus femoris can be traced proximally to its
tendinous attachment to the anterior inferior iliac spine. A tenotomy should be

Figure 4 Images of a right hip show repair of a Pipkin type IV fracture-dislocation via an
anterior approach. A, AP radiograph demonstrates a femoral head fracture-dislocation.
B, Coronal CT scan shows a fracture fragment with the exit point above the fovea. C,
Axial CT scan shows a small posterior wall fracture. D, AP fluoroscopic image shows

mini-fragment interfragmentary screws. E, Stress obturator oblique fluoroscopic image
obtained after fixation of the femoral head shows a concentrically reduced and stable
hip ; therefore, the posterior wall was managed nonsurgically. F, AP radiograph obtained
at 1-year follow-up demonstrates healing of the femoral head without evidence of
osteonecrosis and a stable hip. (Courtesy of L. Henry Goodnough, MD, Seattle, WA.)

Posterior Approach
Via a Gibson or Kocher-Langenbeck interval
Affords access to the femoral head via a surgical hip dislocation and to posterior wall
fragments and tears of the capsule and labrum
Access to the femoral head is provided by performing a digastric trochanteric osteotomy and
surgical hip dislocation.12

Posterior Approach
Either a Gibson or a Kocher-Langenbeck interval can be used. This is performed with the
patient in the lateral position. Surgical hip dislocation allows for circumferential
assessment and access to the femoral head while sparing the blood supply.12-14 The
main advantage of a posterior approach compared with an anterior approach is access
to wall fractures and capsulolabral disruptions. A true Pipkin type IV fracture can be
managed via a single approach using this strategy (Figure 5). In patients with a large
soft-tissue envelope, an orthogonal screw trajectory for the femoral head fracture may
be difficult to attain, given the anteroinferior in location.
Figure 5 Images show repair of a Pipkin type IV fracture-dislocation via a posterior
approach. Anterior (A) and posterior (B) three-dimensional CT reconstruction images of
the pelvis show a right femoral head fracture, a posterior right hip dislocation, and a

fixation of the reduced femoral head fracture with the use of mini-fragment screws, a
digastric osteotomy of the greater trochanter, and surgical dislocation. AP fluoroscopic
images of the right hip show that via a Kocher-Langenbeck approach, the posterior wall
fragment was reduced and provisionally stabilized (D), after which it was definitively
fixed with the use of spring plates and a buttress plate (E). The osteotomy was reduced
and fixed with the use of 3.5-mm solid screws. F, Postoperative AP radiograph of the
pelvis demonstrates anatomic alignment. (Courtesy of L. Henry Goodnough, MD, Seattle,
WA.)
Fixation Options
Reduction strategy and implant selection should account for the goal of anatomic reduction
with rigid fixation without prominence at the chondral articular surface.
To achieve rigid fixation, the authors of this lesson prefer mini-fragment (2.4-mm)
interfragmentary screws, which are countersunk to sit below the level of the chondral
surface.7 Given the characteristic anterior shear fragments, screws often are placed in an
anterior-to-posterior trajectory.
If a femoral neck fracture is present (Pipkin type III), screws should be placed away of the fixed-
angle implant used to manage the neck fracture (Figure 6).
Arthroplasty is an option for Pipkin type III fractures, especially in geriatric individuals (Figure 7).
Combined femoral neck/head fractures represent a very rare subtype of femoral head fracture.
Therefore, knowledge of the natural history of this injury pattern is limited by small case
numbers.
Compared with other femoral head fracture patterns, femoral neck/head fractures are
associated with high rates of fixation failure and osteonecrosis, with complication rates as high as
100%.7
Therefore, arthroplasty is a reasonable alternative to avoid the most common modes of failure
after surgical management of Pipkin type III fractures (Figure 7).
Arthroplasty is also an option in Pipkin I, II, and IV fracture patterns in geriatric patients.

Irreducible Fracture-Dislocations
Irreducible femoral head fracture-dislocations are rare, occur without a posterior wall fracture,
and should be recognized based on clinical and radiographic features.15

Irreducible Fracture-Dislocations
Rarely, femoral head fracture-dislocations occur without a posterior wall fracture, which
are irreducible via closed means and should be recognized based on clinical and
radiographic features.15 Clinically, the patient demonstrates slight locked-hip flexion
with neutral rotation and limb shortening. Plain radiographs and CT scans reveal neutral
rotation of the proximal femur, impaction of the proximal femur on the supra-acetabular
lateral ilium, and no evidence of posterior wall fracture (Figure 8). Failure to identify an
irreducible hip preoperatively may result in iatrogenic femoral neck fracture during a
futile closed reduction attempt.
The authors of this lesson prefer to use a posterior approach for irreducible fracture-
dislocations. To reduce the fracture, the surgeon must identify and incise the taut
posterior capsulolabral tissue through which the head has herniated. Subsequently, the
dislocation can be reduced, and the head can be reduced and fixed as already described.

Complications
Complications after surgical management of femoral head fractures include the following:
Posttraumatic arthritis
Heterotopic ossification
Osteonecrosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Femoral Head Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004094
15/19


Complications
Heterotopic ossification is a common complication; however, reported incidences vary
widely across a large number of studies with small patient numbers. The largest
systematic review reported cumulative rates of 16.8%,16 whereas rates in individual
studies range from 6% to 64%.17 In general, anterior approaches are associated with
higher rates of heterotopic ossification compared with posterior approaches8 (Figure 9).
Osteonecrosis occurs in 8% to 25% of femoral head fractures.5,7 Contemporary studies
potentially underestimate osteonecrosis rates, because minimum follow-up may not
capture late presentations. Advocates of posterior approaches state that the injured
posterior blood supply to the fractured femoral head is further compromised by an
anterior approach, whereas the argument that the femoral head blood supply is
posterior-dominant can be cited to advocate for anterior approaches. Regardless, no
current evidence shows that one approach is more protective against osteonecrosis, and
patients should be counseled that osteonecrosis is a potential complication.
Pipkin type III fractures are associated with high rates of clinical failure caused by loss of
fixation or osteonecrosis. In a small series, the cumulative rate of failure was 100% in
patients with clinical follow-up.7

demonstrates a femoral head fracture. B, Radiograph demonstrates reduction and

Clinical Pearls
The Hueter direct anterior approach and surgical hip dislocation are safe exposures for
reduction and fixation of femoral head fractures.
In Pipkin type IV fractures with an associated posterior wall fracture, initial management
consists of reduction and fixation of the femoral head fracture via a Hueter approach or via
surgical hip dislocation. Subsequently, stability of the posterior wall is assessed via a stress
examination. If the wall fragment is deemed unstable, the posterior wall fracture is then
reduced and fixed.
Beware the irreducible femoral head fracture-dislocation; the surgeon should recognize the
unique clinical and radiographic features of this fracture patten to avoid iatrogenic neck
fracture during attempted closed reduction and should expect abnormal surgical anatomy
during exposure.
Countersunk mini-fragment lag screws are the mainstay of implant selection for femoral neck
fractures.
Arthroplasty should be considered for Pipkin type III femoral head/neck fractures, depending
on the patient’s age.
